feedback: Check: your number of triangles should always be two fewer than the number of sides.
If the quadrilateral gives 360° as two triangles of 180°, you have connected it to the triangle rather than memorised a separate fact.
If you can state WHY a quadrilateral is 360° ('it is two triangles'), you understand the partition, not just the number.
activities.intendedInsight: Every simple polygon's (one with no crossing sides) angle sum is built from triangles: an n-sided polygon divides into (n−2) triangles, so its interior angles sum to (n−2) × 180° — the whole family connects back to the triangle.
learnerActions: Draw a diagonal inside a quadrilateral to split it into two triangles (in a dented, non-convex quadrilateral, use the diagonal that stays inside); conclude its angle sum is 2 × 180° = 360°.
Partition a convex pentagon (3 triangles) and a convex hexagon (4 triangles) from one vertex, counting the triangles each time.
Record results in an angle-sum table: triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°, hexagon 720°.
State the pattern in words and as a rule: an n-gon splits into (n−2) triangles, so its angle sum is (n−2) × 180°.
activities.title: Build the polygon sums by cutting into triangles

feedback: If you subtracted from 360° for a triangle and got 230°, that exceeds 180° — a sign the wrong total was used; a triangle is 180°.
If a figure looks isosceles but the marked angles differ, trust the numbers: 'not drawn to scale' means both appearance AND measuring the drawing are unreliable — only the marked angles are correct.
Writing the subtraction and checking it is reasonable guards against both the wrong-total error and arithmetic slips.
activities.intendedInsight: Missing angles are found by subtracting known angles from the correct total (180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral), using the MARKED values rather than the picture's appearance or a protractor reading of a not-to-scale drawing.
learnerActions: Find a triangle's third angle given two angles by subtracting from 180° (e.g. 180 − (70 + 60) = 50°); write the calculation.
Find a quadrilateral's missing angle by subtracting the three known angles from 360°.
Answer an item deliberately drawn roughly isosceles though it is NOT to scale: compute only from the marked angles, not from how the figure looks and not by measuring the drawing with a protractor.
Sanity-check each answer (each triangle angle must be more than 0° and less than 180°; the three sum to exactly 180°).
activities.title: Missing-angle practice, including 'not drawn to scale'

feedback: If you stopped at 720°, that is the TOTAL of all six angles, not one angle — you still need to divide by 6.
Labelling 'total sum' versus 'one angle' keeps the two steps from collapsing together.
Check scale: one interior angle of a hexagon (120°) should be far smaller than the full 720° total.
activities.intendedInsight: For a regular polygon there are two distinct steps: find the total angle sum, then divide equally among the (equal) vertices to get one interior angle — the total sum is not itself a single angle.
learnerActions: For a regular hexagon, first find the total interior-angle sum (4 triangles × 180° = 720°).
Then, because all six interior angles of a regular hexagon are equal, divide: 720° ÷ 6 = 120° for one interior angle.
Write the two steps separately and label which number is the TOTAL sum and which is ONE angle.
Repeat for another regular polygon (e.g. regular pentagon: 540° ÷ 5 = 108°).
activities.title: Regular polygons: find the sum, THEN share it out
